patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral hand and foot weakness and numbness for 3 years, slow progression, family told to see a specialist
patient.history_present_illness: Harold Watkins is a 56-year-old electrician with a 3-year history of progressive bilateral hand and foot weakness and sensory loss. He has had extensive prior workup attributed his neuropathy to 'mixed diabetic and toxic neuropathy from electrical work' — both of which his current neurologist is questioning. He was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 5 years ago (current HbA1c 7.8%) and his prior physicians attributed his neuropathy to this. He works as an industrial electrician but denies any significant solvent or heavy metal exposures confirmed by occupational health records. He notes that his father was 'basically in a wheelchair at 60 from leg weakness' though he never received a diagnosis. He has two adult children, one of whom (son, age 31) recently complained to his own physician about numb feet. He denies alcohol use. Over the past 6 months, he notes episodic carpal-tunnel-like pain at both wrists that he attributes to his job. He has been wearing bilateral wrist splints. A recent EMG at an outside institution was interpreted as 'length-dependent diabetic axonal neuropathy consistent with history.' He presents now because a podiatry colleague noticed extremely high arches on foot examination and referred him, stating 'this doesn't look like diabetic feet.' He also has prominent muscle wasting in his hands (interossei and thenar) and what he calls 'claw hands' that he attributes to grip fatigue from electrical work. He takes no immune-modulating medications.

specialized_test.impression: ABNORMAL NCS/EMG — uniformly slow demyelinating pattern. Motor conduction velocities uniformly slow throughout all tested nerves bilaterally (27–31 m/s), without focal areas of greater slowing, conduction block, or temporal dispersion. Sensory nerve action potentials reduced or absent bilaterally. Needle EMG: large-amplitude, long-duration, polyphasic motor unit potentials consistent with chronic reinnervation of long duration. Findings indicate a diffuse symmetric demyelinating polyneuropathy with electrophysiological features suggesting hereditary etiology

output.impression: FOCUSED CARPAL TUNNEL NCS: Median palmar latency at wrist: 2.0 ms bilaterally. Median-ulnar palmar latency comparison: difference 0.1 ms (both equally slow, indicating diffuse uniform slowing rather than focal entrapment-related slowing). No median-specific focal slowing at carpal tunnel. Tinel's sign negative bilaterally. CONCLUSION: No electrodiagnostic evidence of carpal tunnel syndrome; the symmetric slowing reflects a diffuse process rather than focal median entrapment. Findings do not support median nerve decompression.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Charcot-Marie-Tooth X-linked type 1 (CMTX1, GJB1) with superimposed diabetic axonal neuropathy

differential.key_features: Most common CMT; uniform very slow velocities; need genetic confirmation to distinguish from CMTX1.
Demyelinating pattern can overlap; CIDP shows non-uniform slowing, conduction block, CSF protein elevation, and responds to immunotherapy.
5-year T2DM HbA1c 7.8% is a real contributor (axonal); does not explain demyelinating pattern or family history.
Recurrent painless mononeuropathies, not symmetric demyelinating; carpal tunnel might be a clue.
Need SPEP/IFE and anti-MAG; would not explain childhood-onset features.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify reversible/treatable etiologies (diabetes, B12 deficiency, monoclonal gammopathy, thyroid disease)

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Length-dependent axonal vs demyelinating vs multifocal pattern; severity and distribution

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Identify potentially neurotoxic drugs (chemotherapy, metronidazole, megadose B6, nitrofurantoin); guide neuropathic-pain pharmacotherapy

optimal_actions.action: Targeted CMT genetic panel (PMP22 duplication, MPZ, GJB1, MFN2)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is a cortical test and is non-contributory in peripheral nerve disease.
Head/brain CT has no role in peripheral neuropathy evaluation.
Brain MRI is not indicated in typical distal symmetric polyneuropathy without CNS signs.
Advanced cerebral imaging (PET/MRA/MRV/perfusion) has no routine role in peripheral neuropathy.
Echocardiography is not indicated unless cardiac amyloid is suspected.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated unless there is syncope or symptomatic dysautonomia with arrhythmia concern.

sequence_constraints.reason: Tier the workup — basic labs first, then targeted electrodiagnostic and tissue studies.

critical_actions: Recognize hereditary demyelinating neuropathy in adult with prior 'carpal tunnel' (often a CMTX1/HNPP forme fruste)
Order CMT genetic panel covering PMP22, MPZ, GJB1 (CMTX1), MFN2
Genetic counseling for X-linked inheritance (CMTX1: males more severe)
contraindicated_actions: Do not treat as CIDP with IVIG before excluding hereditary cause
Do not stop the workup at 'diabetic neuropathy' given demyelinating velocities and family pattern
key_reasoning_points: Demyelinating velocities + insidious chronic course + family pattern = hereditary; genetic confirmation defines subtype and inheritance
Diabetes is a contributor (axonal layer) but not the primary explanation
Bilateral 'carpal tunnel' in this context can be hereditary mononeuropathy at compression sites (HNPP/CMTX1)

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diabetes contributes to axonal layer but cannot explain demyelinating velocities or familial pattern.
May represent forme fruste of hereditary neuropathy (HNPP/CMTX1) — bilateral 'CTS' in a man with demyelinating polyneuropathy should prompt genetic workup.
